lesson.title: Halve a chromosome set

steps.headline: Body cells hold two sets of chromosomes. Gametes hold one.

lead.text: A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent. Matching chromosomes from the two sets are homologous: they carry the same genes.
A gamete, such as an egg or a sperm, is haploid. It has one set.
At fertilisation, two gametes join. Think about what that does to the number of chromosome sets.

reveal.text: You added the two sets. Fertilisation brings two haploid sets together and restores the diploid number.

steps.headline: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

lead.text: Meiosis copies the DNA once, then divides twice.
In the first division, homologous chromosomes are pulled apart. In the second, sister chromatids are pulled apart. The result is four haploid cells.

steps.headline: A cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does each cell have after both divisions?

workedSteps.text: Meiosis I sends one chromosome of each pair to each cell.
Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. The count stays at 3 in each of four cells.

steps.headline: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. How many chromosomes does each final cell have?

workedSteps.text: Meiosis I sends one chromosome of each pair to each cell.
Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. Count one chromosome from each pair.

lead.text: DNA is copied once at the start of meiosis. The cell then divides twice. Check what happens between the two divisions.

reveal.text: You counted no new copying. Two divisions share one round of copying, which is why the number halves.

lead.text: Two siblings have the same parents and the same chromosome count, yet they are not identical. Meiosis shuffles chromosomes, and chromosomes can swap segments.

reveal.text: Assortment and crossing over make every gamete different. The simple count diagram leaves crossing over out.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish homologues from sister chromatids and follow two meiotic divisions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. An egg and a sperm join to make the first cell of a baby.
That first cell must have 46 chromosomes too.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow chromosome numbers through the two divisions of meiosis and fertilisation.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why each child is a mix of both parents.

recap.keyIdea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, so gametes are haploid. Fertilisation restores diploid cells with a new mix of chromosomes.

blocks.text: You found that an egg carries 23 chromosomes and that a 3-pair cell gives gametes with 3. You also saw no copying between the divisions.

recap.nextHook: Now follow a single gene through a cross. What could the offspring inherit?

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does it contain before DNA replication?
hints: Each pair contains two homologues.
There are three pairs.
Multiply the pairs by the chromosomes in each.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Each homologous pair holds two chromosomes, so count them in twos.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Each pair holds two chromosomes.
Replication has not happened yet, so nothing has been doubled.

questions.prompt: Meiosis I separates one kind of chromosome relationship. Name the paired chromosomes it pulls apart.
hints: The pair holds matching chromosomes from the two sets.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate first; sister chromatids remain joined.

questions.onCorrect: Homologous chromosomes. Pulling them apart is what halves the chromosome number.

misconceptions.feedback: Sister chromatids stay joined in meiosis I. They part in the second division.

questions.prompt: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. After the two meiotic divisions, how many chromosomes does each final cell have?
hints: Meiosis reduces two chromosome sets to one.
The starting cell has two homologous pairs.
Take one chromosome from each pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each final haploid cell has one from each pair: two chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each final cell holds one chromosome from each pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the starting number. Each final cell has only one set.
A final cell has one from each pair, and there are two pairs.

questions.prompt: Two gametes each contain 3 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in their diploid fertilisation product?
hints: Fertilisation combines the two sets.
Each gamete supplies three chromosomes.
Add the two contributions.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Two haploid sets combine to restore a diploid cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one gamete's contribution. Fertilisation brings two together.
Each gamete supplies three, so add only those two amounts.

questions.prompt: How many additional DNA-replication rounds normally occur between meiosis I and meiosis II?
hints: Trace the copied chromosomes through both divisions.
Meiosis begins with one replication round.
Between the divisions, the DNA is divided again without being recopied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No additional replication occurs; the second division separates existing sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The second division separates the copies already made, so the amount of DNA halves again.

misconceptions.feedback: That round happens once, before meiosis I. None happens between the divisions.
Each division is a separation, not a copying.

questions.prompt: Why can siblings inherit different chromosome combinations?
hints: Chromosome counts can match while the combinations differ.

acceptedIdeas: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assortment and crossing over produce varied gametes; the simple count diagram omits crossover.

choices.label: Each parent has no genetic variation
Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis

questions.onCorrect: Chromosomes assort and swap segments, so every gamete carries a different mix.

misconceptions.feedback: Parents carry different versions of genes on their chromosomes.
Gametes differ from one another because of how meiosis shuffles chromosomes.

questions.prompt: A human gamete has 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human body cell have?
hints: A gamete holds one set.
A body cell holds two sets.
Double the gamete's number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A body cell is diploid, with two sets: 2 × 23 = 46.

questions.onCorrect: 46. A body cell is diploid, so it holds twice the number a gamete holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one set. A body cell has two.
That doubles twice. A body cell holds just two sets.

questions.prompt: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. What does meiosis II separate?
hints: Think of the two joined copies of each chromosome.
questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They are the joined copies made before meiosis I.

misconceptions.feedback: Those were already separated in meiosis I. Name the structures that remain joined.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does each gamete made from it have?
hints: A gamete holds one chromosome set.
The diploid cell holds two sets.
Halve the diploid number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A gamete is haploid, with half the diploid number: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Meiosis halves the number so each gamete has one set.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the diploid number. A gamete holds half of it.
That halves twice. Meiosis halves the number once overall.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes does the egg carry?
hints: Each parent supplies the same number.
The two contributions must add up to the baby's total.
Share the baby's total equally between egg and sperm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The egg and sperm each supply half of 46: 46 ÷ 2 = 23.

questions.onCorrect: 23. Gametes carry half the usual number, so that fertilisation restores the full number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the full number. If the egg carried 46 and the sperm carried 46, the baby would have double.
That is what you would get if both gametes carried a full set.

questions.prompt: Why does the chromosome number halve in meiosis I and not in meiosis II?
hints: Think about which relationship is separated in each division.

acceptedIdeas: Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In meiosis I each daughter gets one chromosome from each homologous pair, so the number halves.

choices.label: Meiosis II copies the DNA again
Homologous chromosomes go to different cells in meiosis I
DNA is destroyed in meiosis I

questions.onCorrect: Each cell gets one chromosome from each pair in meiosis I. Meiosis II only separates the copies.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no second copying. Meiosis II divides the existing copies.
No DNA is destroyed. Each chromosome goes to one daughter cell.
